On the integrality of some P-recursive sequences

Anastasia Matveeva
Abstract

This project investigates the arithmetic nature of P-recursive sequences through the lens of their D-finite generating functions. Building on classical tools from differential algebra, we revisit the integrality criterion for Motzkin-type sequences due to Klazar and Luca, and propose a unified method for analysing global boundedness and algebraicity within a broader class of holonomic sequences. The central contribution is an algorithm that determines whether all, none, or a one-dimensional family of solutions to certain second-order recurrences are globally bounded. This approach generalizes earlier ad hoc methods and applies successfully to several well-known sequences from the OEIS.

1 Introduction

Definition 1.1.

A sequence (un)n∈ℕ(u_{n})_{n\in\mathbb{N}} of rational numbers is called P-recursive (or P-finite, or holonomic) if it satisfies a linear (homogeneous) recurrence relation with coefficients in ℚ⁡[n]\mathbb{Q}[n].

Definition 1.2.

A power series f∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is called D-finite (‘‘differentially finite’’, or ‘‘holonomic’’) if it satisfies a linear (homogeneous) differential equation with coefficients in ℚ⁡[x]\mathbb{Q}[x].

Theorem 1.3.

([Sta80, Theorem 1.5]) A power series is D-finite if and only if its coefficient sequence is P-recursive.

Definition 1.4.

A power series f⁡(x)=∑n≥0an​xn∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}a_{n}x^{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is called almost integral if there exists C∈ℤ∗C\in\mathbb{Z}^{*} such that f⁡(C​x)−f⁡(0)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]f(Cx)-f(0)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]]. Equivalently, if there exists C∈ℤ∗C\in\mathbb{Z}^{*} such that Cn​an∈ℤC^{n}a_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n≥1n\geq 1.

Definition 1.5.

A power series f∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is called globally bounded if it is almost integral and has a nonzero radius of convergence in ℂ\mathbb{C}.

P‑recursive sequences appear in many combinatorics problems, as well as in number theory and the theory of special functions. Whether a given P‑recursive sequence consists of integers only is a deceptively simple question, which is often approached with arguments tailored for particular sequences. Our starting point is the family of Motzkin‑type sequences (defined properly in Section 2), that is, of sequences that satisfy

(n+2)​mn=(2​n+1)​mn−1+(3​n−3)​mn−2.(n+2)m_{n}=(2n+1)m_{n-1}+(3n-3)m_{n-2}.

with arbitrary initial values m0,m1∈ℚm_{0},m_{1}\in\mathbb{Q}.

In Section 2, we discuss the approach of Klazar and Luca to the integrality of Motzkin-type sequences and provide an algebraic argument for the integrality of Motzkin numbers. Section 3 generalizes this to a full characterisation of algebraicity and global boundedness for the entire Motzkin-type family. In Section 4, we present an algorithm that decides these properties for an even larger family of second-order P-recursive sequences with polynomial coefficients of degree 1, under certain assumptions on the recurrence coefficients. The algorithm is then applied to several sequences from the OEIS, including large Schröder numbers and central trinomial coefficients. The integrality question is explored in Section 5. Finally, in Section 6, we derive integrality criteria for small Apéry numbers, by adapting different approaches from the literature.

2 Integrality analysis of Motzkin-type sequences

A Motzkin-type sequence M⁡(μ,λ)=(mn​(μ,λ))nM(\mu,\lambda)=(m_{n}(\mu,\lambda))_{n} is defined in [KL05] as a sequence of rational numbers that satisfies the recurrence:

(n+2)​mn​(μ,λ)=(2​n+1)​mn−1​(μ,λ)+(3​n−3)​mn−2​(μ,λ).(n+2)m_{n}(\mu,\lambda)=(2n+1)m_{n-1}(\mu,\lambda)+(3n-3)m_{n-2}(\mu,\lambda). (1.1)

with initial values m0​(μ,λ)=μm_{0}(\mu,\lambda)=\mu, m1​(μ,λ)=λm_{1}(\mu,\lambda)=\lambda. By abuse of notation, we sometimes write mnm_{n} instead of mn​(μ,λ)m_{n}(\mu,\lambda) when it is clear which initial values are considered.

In particular, M⁡(1,1)M(1,1) is the sequence of Motzkin numbers (A001006 in the OEIS). These numbers have a few interesting combinatorial interpretations, the most well-known being in terms of lattice paths. Motzkin numbers count the number of paths in the Cartesian plane from (0,0)(0,0) to (n,0)(n,0) that never dip below the horizontal axis and consist of up (1,1)(1,1), down (1,−1)(1,-1), and level (1,0)(1,0) steps — known as Motzkin paths. They are also closely related to Catalan numbers, which count the special case where level steps are not allowed (Dyck paths).

In [KL05] Klazar and Luca prove that M⁡(μ,λ)M(\mu,\lambda) is integral, that is, consists of integers only, if and only if μ,λ∈ℤ\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb{Z} and μ=λ\mu=\lambda. In this section we provide a summary of their approach and discuss its limitations.

2.1 Approach of Klazar and Luca

One starts by deducing the integrality of M⁡(μ,μ)=μ​M​(1,1)M(\mu,\mu)=\mu M(1,1) for μ∈ℤ\mu\in\mathbb{Z}. This is nothing more than a straightforward corollary of the integrality of M⁡(1,1)M(1,1). If μ∉ℤ\mu\notin\mathbb{Z}, then M⁡(μ,μ)∉ℤ⁡[[x]]M(\mu,\mu)\notin\mathbb{Z}[[x]] as its first coefficient μ\mu is already not an integer. Regarding the case M⁡(μ,λ)M(\mu,\lambda) with μ≠λ\mu\neq\lambda, the following result holds, where P⁡(k)P(k) denotes the largest prime factor of k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z} with the convention that P⁡(0)=P⁡(±1)=1P(0)=P(\pm 1)=1.

Theorem 2.1.

([KL05], Theorem 1). Let M⁡(μ,λ)=(mn​(μ,λ))n≥0=(mn)n≥0M(\mu,\lambda)=(m_{n}(\mu,\lambda))_{n\geq 0}=(m_{n})_{n\geq 0} be any Motzkin-type sequence of rational numbers with m0=μ≠λ=m1m_{0}=\mu\neq\lambda=m_{1}. For any nn write mn=anbnm_{n}=\frac{a_{n}}{b_{n}}, where ana_{n} and bnb_{n} are coprime integers with bn≥1b_{n}\geq 1. Then limsupn→∞\lim\sup_{n\rightarrow\infty} P⁡(bn)=∞P(b_{n})=\infty.

In other words, if μ≠λ\mu\neq\lambda, then for infinitely many primes pp there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that mn​(μ,λ)m_{n}(\mu,\lambda) has a denominator divisible by pp. Moreover, it can be shown that for pp large enough it is in fact mp−2​(μ,λ)m_{p-2}(\mu,\lambda) that has a denominator divisible by pp.

Below is a concise summary of the proof of Theorem 2.1. We refer to [KL05] for more details.

Proof strategy for Theorem 2.1. It suffices to exhibit a single pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) with α≠β\alpha\neq\beta such that M⁡(α,β)M(\alpha,\beta) contains terms whose denominators are divisible by arbitrarily large primes, since the set of solutions to (1.1) is two-dimensional. Indeed, every sequence M⁡(a,b)M(a,b) can be written as a linear combination of M⁡(1,1)M(1,1) and M⁡(α,β)M(\alpha,\beta). Since M⁡(1,1)M(1,1) is integral, M⁡(a,b)M(a,b) is almost integral for a≠ba\neq b if and only if M⁡(α,β)M(\alpha,\beta) is.

To construct an easy-to-work-with example, consider the shifted generating power series M⁡(x)=∑n≥0mn​xn+2M(x)=\sum_{n\geq 0}m_{n}x^{n+2} and complete it to a power series S⁡(x)=a+b​x+M⁡(x)S(x)=a+bx+M(x) that satisfies an inhomogeneous linear differential equation of order 1. With a clever choice of a,b,m0,m1a,b,m_{0},m_{1}, this differential equation rewrites as

g​S′−12​g′​S=g,where ​g​(x)=1−2​x−3​x2.gS^{\prime}-\tfrac{1}{2}g^{\prime}S=g,\quad\text{where }g(x)=1-2x-3x^{2}. (1.2)

This equation admits the solution

S⁡(x)=g⁡(x)​∫1g⁡(x)​𝑑x,S(x)=\sqrt{g(x)}\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{g(x)}}\,dx,

whose coefficients mkm_{k} satisfy

mk−2=∑n=0k−1cn​dk−n−1k−n=dk−1k+∑n=1k−1cn​dk−n−1k−n,for all ​k≥2,m_{k-2}=\sum_{n=0}^{k-1}\frac{c_{n}d_{k-n-1}}{k-n}=\frac{d_{k-1}}{k}+\sum_{n=1}^{k-1}\frac{c_{n}d_{k-n-1}}{k-n},\quad\text{for all }k\geq 2,

where cnc_{n} and dnd_{n} are the coefficients of the power series expansions of g⁡(x)=1+∑n≥1cn​xn\sqrt{g(x)}=1+\sum\limits_{n\geq 1}c_{n}x^{n} and 1/g⁡(x)=1+∑n≥1dn​xn1/\sqrt{g(x)}=1+\sum\limits_{n\geq 1}d_{n}x^{n}, respectively. Both (cn)n(c_{n})_{n} and (dn)n(d_{n})_{n} are integer sequences.

The crucial point is that dp−1d_{p-1} is not divisible by pp for any prime p>3p>3. This is established by analysing the explicit binomial sum representation of 1+∑n≥1dn​xn1+\sum\limits_{n\geq 1}d_{n}x^{n}. As a result, mp−2m_{p-2} has a denominator divisible by pp for large pp, and since pp is arbitrary, Theorem 2.1 follows. ∎

2.2 Discussion

A natural question to ask is:

To what extent can the approach described in [KL05] be generalized and applied to other P-recursive sequences?

Comment 1. The first claim made by Klazar and Luca is the integrality of Motzkin-type sequences of the form M⁡(μ,μ)M(\mu,\mu), μ∈ℤ\mu\in\mathbb{Z}. Although the argument appears to be direct, it relies heavily on the combinatorial properties of M⁡(1,1)M(1,1). Hence, the first limitation: in the general case the underlying combinatorial interpretation (if any) of a given P-recursive sequence is not known beforehand. This already arises two questions:

  1. 1.1

    How to ‘‘guess’’ that the choice m0=m1=1m_{0}=m_{1}=1 results in an integral solution of (1.1)?

  2. 1.2

    How to prove it?

Question 1.1 can be approached algorithmically with the approach presented in Section 4.2.

One way to answer question 1.2 is to consider the generating function y⁡(x)=∑n≥0mn​xny(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}m_{n}x^{n}. Its coefficient sequence is P-recursive thanks to (1.1), so we know that y⁡(x)y(x) is D-finite. Let us carry out some computations in Maple11 1 Using the gfun package, version 4.10.

> rec := {(n + 2)m(n) = (2n + 1)m(n - 1) + (3n - 3)m(n - 2), m(0) = 1,  m(1)= 1} :
> with(gfun):
> rectodiffeq(rec, m(n), y(x));
(−3​x2−3​x+2)​y​(x)+(−3​x3−2​x2+x)​(dd​x​y​(x))−2.(-3x^{2}-3x+2)y(x)+(-3x^{3}-2x^{2}+x)\left(\frac{d}{dx}y(x)\right)-2. 
> dsolve({%, y(0) = 1}, y(x));
y⁡(x)=I​3​x−1​x+1−x+12​x2.y(x)=\frac{I\sqrt{3x-1}\sqrt{x+1}-x+1}{2x^{2}}.

y⁡(x)=1−x−1−2​x−3​x22​x2.y(x)=\frac{1-x-\sqrt{1-2x-3x^{2}}}{2x^{2}}.

and one recognizes the closed form for the generating function of Motzkin numbers.

Remark 2.2.

The above reasoning could have been made shorter by appealing to known identities for Motzkin numbers. For example, one could argue that

m⁡(x)=1−x−1−2​x−3​x22​x2m(x)=\frac{1-x-\sqrt{1-2x-3x^{2}}}{2x^{2}}

is a standard way of expressing terms of M⁡(1,1)M(1,1) and therefore the computation by hand (or within a computer algebra system) is redundant. However, most of such results utilize implicitly the connections with combinatorial objects and this is precisely what we are trying to avoid for the sake of generality.

Comment 2. It is noteworthy that the proof of Theorem 2.1 depends significantly on the structure of the differential equation (1.2). As a result, even slight changes to the recurrence parameters require adjustments to the method.

In view of Definition 1.5, and using the fact that M⁡(μ,μ)M(\mu,\mu) is globally bounded (because it belongs to μ​ℤ​[[x]]\mu\mathbb{Z}[[x]]) for any μ∈ℚ\mu\in\mathbb{Q}, we can reformulate Theorem 2.1 as follows:

Theorem 2.3.

A Motzkin-type sequence M⁡(μ,λ)M(\mu,\lambda) with μ,λ∈ℚ\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb{Q} is globally bounded if and only if μ=λ\mu=\lambda.

Let us now invoke an important result, first stated by Eisenstein in 1852 ([Eis52]) and subsequently proved by Heine ([Hei53], [Hei54]):

Theorem 2.4.

(Eisenstein’s theorem). If f⁡(x)∈ℚ⁡[[x]]f(x)\in\mathbb{Q}[[x]] is algebraic, then it is globally bounded.

Using the fact that the generating function of Motzkin numbers (and, consequently, of any M⁡(μ,μ)M(\mu,\mu) by linearity) is algebraic, we obtain the following corollary:

Corollary 2.5.

(of Theorem 2.3 and Theorem 2.4) The generating function of a Motzkin-type sequence M⁡(μ,λ)M(\mu,\lambda) is algebraic if and only if μ=λ\mu=\lambda.

3 Arithmetic outlook

We recall that Motzkin-type sequences satisfy the recurrence

(n+2)​mn=(2​n+1)​mn−1+(3​n−3)​mn−2,n≥2(n+2)m_{n}=(2n+1)m_{n-1}+(3n-3)m_{n-2},\quad n\geq 2 (2.1)

and are uniquely defined by a pair of initial values m0,m1m_{0},m_{1}. We will also write mn​(λ,μ)m_{n}(\lambda,\mu) for the nnth term of a Motzkin-type sequence with m0=μ,m1=λm_{0}=\mu,m_{1}=\lambda when it is necessary to specify the initial values.

In what follows, we will also make use of the notion of diagonals of multivariate power series:

Definition 3.1.

Let

R⁡(x1,…,xk)=∑n1,…,nk≥0c⁡(n1,…,nk)​x1n1​…​xknk∈ℚ⁡[[x1,…,xk]].R(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})=\sum\limits_{n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}\geq 0}c(n_{1},\ldots,n_{k})x_{1}^{n_{1}}\ldots x_{k}^{n_{k}}\in\mathbb{Q}[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}]].

The diagonal of RR is a univariate power series defined by

Diag​(R)=∑n≥0c⁡(n,…,n)​tn∈ℚ⁡[[t]].\text{Diag}(R)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}c(n,\ldots,n)t^{n}\in\mathbb{Q}[[t]].
Proposition 3.2.

(Furstenberg, [Fur67]). Any algebraic power series is the diagonal of a rational function in two variables.

The converse of Proposition 3.2, known as Pólya’s theorem [Pó22], is also true.

Proposition 3.3.

([Chr90, Proposition 5, p. 49]) Diagonals of rational functions are globally bounded.

Set M⁡(x)=∑n≥0mn​xnM(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}m_{n}x^{n}. The next result describes several equivalent conditions involving the arithmetic nature of M⁡(x)M(x), and the parameters defining the sequence (mn)n(m_{n})_{n}.

Theorem 3.4.

The following statements are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    M⁡(x)M(x) is algebraic.

  2. 2.

    M⁡(x)M(x) is globally bounded.

  3. 3.

    There exists b∈ℤ∗b\in\mathbb{Z}^{*} such that mn∈1b​ℤm_{n}\in\frac{1}{b}\mathbb{Z} for all n≥0n\geq 0.

  4. 4.

    m0=m1m_{0}=m_{1}.

  5. 5.

    M⁡(x)M(x) is a diagonal of some bivariate rational function.

Proof.

  1. 1⟹21\implies 2.

    By Eisenstein’s theorem.

  2. 2⟹42\implies 4.

    By the contrapositive of Theorem 2.3.

  3. 1⇔41\iff 4.

    By Corollary 2.5.

  4. 4⟹34\implies 3.

    By the fact that the sequence of Motzkin numbers, i.e. (mn​(1,1))n(m_{n}(1,1))_{n}, is integral and mn​(ab,ab)=ab​mn​(1,1)m_{n}(\frac{a}{b},\frac{a}{b})=\frac{a}{b}m_{n}(1,1) for all n≥0n\geq 0 and all a,b∈ℤa,b\in\mathbb{Z}.

  5. 3⟹23\implies 2.

    Trivial.

  6. 1⟹51\implies 5.

    By Proposition 3.2.

  7. 5⟹25\implies 2.

    By Proposition 3.3.

∎

The figure below visualizes the implications in Theorem 3.4:

Such a result is surprising as it establishes, in the case of this specific recurrence, the converse of Eisenstein’s theorem (the implication 1. ⟹\implies 2.). Of course, this is no longer true in the general setting, and there are many examples of transcendental functions with almost integral, or even integral power series expansions. For instance, the generating function of the squared central binomial coefficients lives in ℤ⁡[[x]]\mathbb{Z}[[x]], but at the same time is transcendental ([Fur67, p. 271–272]). It writes as

F12​[12​12 1; 16​x]=∑n≥0(2​nn)2​xn,{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left[\!\begin{array}[]{c}\ \frac{1}{2}\ \frac{1}{2}\\ \ 1\end{array};\,16x\right]=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}\binom{2n}{n}^{2}x^{n},

where F12{}_{2}F_{1} denotes the Gaussian hypergeometric function defined as

F12​[abc;x]=∑n=0∞(a)n​(b)n(c)n​xnn!,{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left[\!\begin{array}[]{c}\ a\ \ b\\ \ c\end{array};\,x\right]=\sum\limits_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_{n}(b)_{n}}{(c)_{n}}\frac{x^{n}}{n!},

and (q)n(q)_{n} is the rising factorial (also known as Pochhammer symbol):

(q)n={1if ​n=0,q⁡(q+1)​…​(q+n−1)if ​n>0.(q)_{n}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }n=0,\\ q(q+1)\ldots(q+n-1)&\text{if }n>0.\end{cases}

There is no contradiction with the general falsity of the converse. At a closer look, the equivalence of 1. and 2. relies on an intermediate step: namely the condition m0=m1m_{0}=m_{1}. The phenomenon is captured by the chain of implications 1⟹2⟹41\implies 2\implies 4.

Another curious observation is that the implication 2⟹52\implies 5 entails Christol’s conjecture ([Chr90], Conjecture 4, p. 55) for P-recursive sequences that are solutions of (2.1).

Conjecture 3.5.

([Chr90]) Every D-finite globally bounded function is the diagonal of a rational function.

It is worth mentioning that Theorem 3.4 is not easily generalizable to other linear recurrences. Even in the very specific case of second-order recurrences, the implications 2⟹12\implies 1 and 3⟹13\implies 1 do not hold if we drop the linearity of polynomial coefficients. As a counterexample one can take the recurrence for big Apéry numbers (OEIS A005259):

n3​An=(34​n3−51​n2+27​n−5)​An−1−(n−1)3​An−2.n^{3}A_{n}=(34n^{3}-51n^{2}+27n-5)A_{n-1}-(n-1)^{3}A_{n-2}. (2.2)

The sequence solving the recurrence above with A0=1,A1=5A_{0}=1,A_{1}=5 appears in Apéry’s famous proof of the irrationality of ζ⁡(3)\zeta(3) ([Apé79]), and is known to be integral. Integrality can be deduced, for example, from the binomial sums representation of (An)n(A_{n})_{n}:

An=∑k=0n(nk)2​(n+kk)2,n∈ℕ.A_{n}=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{n+k}{k}^{2},\quad n\in\mathbb{N}.

There exist several proofs of the fact that A0=1,A1=5A_{0}=1,A_{1}=5 is the only pair of initial values (up to multiplication by an integer) that produces an integer sequence ([Cha84], [AJ91]). However, the generating function ∑n≥0An​xn\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}A_{n}x^{n} of any sequence that solves (2.2) is transcendental (one reason for this is asymptotics incompatible with algebraicity, the so-called Flajolet criterion).

A similar argument applies to small Apéry numbers (OEIS A005258): the generating function of any sequence produced by the recurrence for small Apéry numbers is transcendental, while there do exist almost integral and even integral solutions of this recurrence. A detailed analysis of such cases is provided in Section 6.

4 Bridging global boundedness and algebraicity

One possible generalization of Theorem 3.4 is the following one, which we state as a conjecture:

Conjecture 4.1.

Let (sn)n(s_{n})_{n} be a sequence of rational numbers that satisfies a linear homogeneous recurrence relation with polynomial coefficients of degree 1:

∑k=0d(akn+bk)sn−k=0,ai≠0 for i=0,…,dd∈ℕ.\sum\limits_{k=0}^{d}(a_{k}n+b_{k})s_{n-k}=0,\quad a_{i}\neq 0\text{ for }i=0,\ldots,d\quad d\in\mathbb{N}.

Let S⁡(x)=∑n≥0sn​xnS(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}s_{n}x^{n} be its generating function. The following statements are equivalent:

  1. 1.

    S⁡(x)S(x) is algebraic.

  2. 2.

    S⁡(x)S(x) is a diagonal.

  3. 3.

    S⁡(x)S(x) is globally bounded.

As before,

1⟹21\implies 2 by Proposition 3.2,

2⟹32\implies 3 by Proposition 3.3.

The interesting direction is 3⟹13\implies 1. We prove it for first-order recurrences in Section 4.1 and for a specific subclass of second-order recurrences in Section 4.2. The general case of Conjecture 4.1 is currently unsolved.

4.1 Hypergeometric case

The most basic setting of Conjecture 4.1 is the case d=1d=1. It defines a certain subclass of hypergeometric functions, that is, of power series whose coefficient sequences satisfy first-order linear recurrences with polynomial coefficients. Specifically, we consider (sn)n(s_{n})_{n} such that

(a0​n+b0)​sn+(a1​n+b1)​sn−1=0,a0,a1∈ℤ∗,b0,b1∈ℤ,b0a0∉−ℕ∗.(a_{0}n+b_{0})s_{n}+(a_{1}n+b_{1})s_{n-1}=0,\quad a_{0},a_{1}\in\mathbb{Z}^{*},\quad b_{0},b_{1}\in\mathbb{Z},\quad\frac{b_{0}}{a_{0}}\not\in-\mathbb{N}^{*}.

Or, equivalently

(n+b0)​sn+(a1​n+b1)​sn−1=0,a1∈ℚ∗,b0∈ℚ∖−ℕ∗,b1∈ℚ,(n+b_{0})s_{n}+(a_{1}n+b_{1})s_{n-1}=0,\quad a_{1}\in\mathbb{Q}^{*},\quad b_{0}\in\mathbb{Q}\setminus-\mathbb{N}^{*},\quad b_{1}\in\mathbb{Q}, (3.1)

where the condition b0a0∉−ℕ∗\frac{b_{0}}{a_{0}}\not\in-\mathbb{N}^{*} comes from the fact that if a0​n+b0=0a_{0}n+b_{0}=0 for some n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, then sns_{n} is undefined unless sk=0s_{k}=0 for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}.

Let S⁡(x)=∑n≥0sn​xnS(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}s_{n}x^{n} denote the generating function of (sn)n(s_{n})_{n}.

The usual scheme of transforming (3.1) into a differential equation and then solving it yields:

S⁡(x)=x−b0​(a1​x+1)−1+b0−b1a1​(s0​b0​∫x−1+b0​(a1​x+1)−a1​b0+b1a1​𝑑x+c1).S(x)=x^{-b_{0}}(a_{1}x+1)^{-1+b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}}\left(s_{0}b_{0}\int x^{-1+b_{0}}(a_{1}x+1)^{\frac{-a_{1}b_{0}+b_{1}}{a_{1}}}dx+c_{1}\right). (3.2)

We can clearly see that S⁡(x)S(x) is a combination of algebraic functions and a primitive of an algebraic function

x−1+b0​(a1​x+1)−a1​b0+b1a1.x^{-1+b_{0}}(a_{1}x+1)^{\frac{-a_{1}b_{0}+b_{1}}{a_{1}}}.

Fortunately, the problem of integrating algebraic functions has been extensively studied and goes back to the work of Liouville [Lüt12, Chapter IX]. In our analysis we make use of the following (rather involved) theorem due to André:

Theorem 4.2.

(André, [And89, p. 149]). Let yy be a power series. Then yy is algebraic if and only if yy is globally bounded and d​yd​x\frac{dy}{dx} is algebraic.

Corollary 4.3.

(of Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 2.4). The primitive of an algebraic power series is globally bounded if and only if it is algebraic.

Therefore, S⁡(x)S(x) is algebraic if and only if it is globally bounded, which immediately implies Conjecture 4.1 for this case d=1d=1.

The next theorem characterises the conditions under which S⁡(x)S(x) is algebraic and globally bounded, noting that these properties are equivalent by Conjecture 4.1.

Theorem 4.4.

Let (sn)n(s_{n})_{n} be a sequence of rational numbers that satisfies (3.1). Then the generating function S⁡(x)=∑n≥0sn​xnS(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}s_{n}x^{n} is globally bounded (and algebraic) if and only if one of the following conditions holds:

  1. 1.

    b0∈ℕ,b1a1∉ℤb_{0}\in\mathbb{N},\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\notin\mathbb{Z}, or

  2. 2.

    b0∉ℤ,b0−b1a1∈−ℕb_{0}\notin\mathbb{Z},\ b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\in-\mathbb{N}, or

  3. 3.

    b0,b0−b1a1∉ℤ,b1a1+1∈−ℕb_{0},b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\notin\mathbb{Z},\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}+1\in-\mathbb{N}, or

  4. 4.

    b0,b1a1∈ℤ,b1a1<0<b0,b1a1≤−1b_{0},\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\in\mathbb{Z},\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}<0<b_{0},\ \frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\leq-1, or

  5. 5.

    b0,b1a1∈ℤ, 0<b0≤b1a1b_{0},\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\in\mathbb{Z},\ 0<b_{0}\leq\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}.

S⁡(x)=x−b0​(a1​x+1)−1+b0−b1a1​(s0​xb0​F12​[b0b0−b1a11+b0;−a1​x]+c1).S(x)=x^{-b_{0}}(a_{1}x+1)^{-1+b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}}\left(s_{0}x^{b_{0}}{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left[\!\begin{array}[]{c}b_{0}\quad b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\\ 1+b_{0}\end{array};\,-a_{1}x\right]+c_{1}\right). (3.3)

An algorithm to determine the algebraicity of hypergeometric functions with arbitrary parameters is described by Fürnsinn and Yurkevich in [FY24]. In the same paper, a useful criterion for deciding the algebraicity of Gaussian hypergeometric functions is presented:

Corollary 4.5.

([FY24], Corollary 3.7)
The Gaussian hypergeometric function F12​([α,β],[α+k],x){}_{2}F_{1}\!\bigl([\alpha,\beta],[\,\alpha+k];x\bigr) for k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, is algebraic if and only if either k≤0k\leq 0 or:

    α∉ℤ,β∈−ℕ\alpha\notin\mathbb{Z},\ \beta\in-\mathbb{N}, or

In our case of F12​[b0b0−b1a11+b0;−a1​x]{}_{2}F_{1}\left[\!\begin{array}[]{c}b_{0}\quad b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\\ 1+b_{0}\end{array};\,-a_{1}x\right], the values are α=b0,β=b0−b1a1,k=1\alpha=b_{0},\beta=b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}},k=1. By substituting them into Corollary 4.5, we obtain the necessary and sufficient conditions for the algebraicity of S⁡(x)S(x), captured in Theorem 4.4.

Observe that case 4. in Corollary 4.5 is not possible for the choice α=b0,β=b0−b1a1,k=1\alpha=b_{0},\beta=b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}},k=1. Indeed, the three requirements in that line become

b0,b1a1∈ℤ,b0<b0−b1a1≤0,−b1a1≥1.b_{0},\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\in\mathbb{Z},\quad b_{0}<b_{0}-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\leq 0,\quad-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\geq 1.

Given a recurrence of type (4.1), a sequence (sn)n(s_{n})_{n} is uniquely defined by a pair (s0,s1)(s_{0},s_{1}). The algebraic nature of S⁡(x)S(x) falls therefore into one of three cases:

      ci\displaystyle c_{i} =−ci+2​(i+2)+ci+1​a1​(i+2+q)a2​(i+2+2​q),i=0,…,n−3,i≠−2q−2,\displaystyle=-\frac{c_{i+2}(i+2)+c_{i+1}a_{1}\left(i+2+q\right)}{a_{2}(i+2+2q)},\quad i=0,\ldots,n-3,\ i\neq-2q-2,
      c−2​q−2\displaystyle c_{-2q-2} =0(could be any value),\displaystyle=0\quad\text{(could be any value)},
      c\displaystyle c =−c1−a1​c0​(q+1),\displaystyle=-c_{1}-a_{1}c_{0}(q+1),
      c~\displaystyle\tilde{c} =2​q​c−2​q+a1​q​c−2​q−1.\displaystyle=2qc_{-2q}+a_{1}qc_{-2q-1}.

      If n=−2​qn=-2q:

      c−2​q−1\displaystyle c_{-2q-1} =1a2,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{a_{2}},
      c−2​q−2\displaystyle c_{-2q-2} =0(could be any value),\displaystyle=0\quad\text{(could be any value)},
      ci\displaystyle c_{i} =−ci+2​(i+2)+ci+1​a1​(i+2+q)a2​(i+2+2​q),i=0,…,−2q−3,\displaystyle=-\frac{c_{i+2}(i+2)+c_{i+1}a_{1}\left(i+2+q\right)}{a_{2}(i+2+2q)},\quad i=0,\ldots,-2q-3,
      c\displaystyle c =−c1−a1​c0​(q+1),\displaystyle=-c_{1}-a_{1}c_{0}(q+1),
      c~\displaystyle\tilde{c} =a1​q​c−2​q−1.\displaystyle=a_{1}qc_{-2q-1}.
  4. 4.

    𝐧≥𝟏,𝐪∈−ℕ∗\mathbf{n\geq 1,q\in-\mathbb{N}^{*}}. Since the double root case was treated earlier, we may assume

    1+a1​x+a2​x2=(1+α​x)​(1+β​x),α≠β.1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2}=(1+\alpha x)(1+\beta x),\ \alpha\neq\beta.

    Moreover, α,β≠0\alpha,\beta\neq 0. Apply a partial fraction decomposition to the integrand:

    xn(1+a1​x+a2​x2)−q=xn(1+α​x)−q​(1+β​x)−q=∑m=1−q(Am(1+α​x)m+Bm(1+β​x)m).\frac{x^{n}}{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{-q}}=\frac{x^{n}}{(1+\alpha x)^{-q}(1+\beta x)^{-q}}=\sum\limits_{m=1}^{-q}\left(\frac{A_{m}}{(1+\alpha x)^{m}}+\frac{B_{m}}{(1+\beta x)^{m}}\right). (4.8)

    Where AmA_{m} and BmB_{m} are coefficients to be determined. Let us integrate the sum in (4.8):

    ∫xn(1+a1​x+a2​x2)−q​𝑑x=∫∑m=1−q(Am(1+α​x)m+Bm(1+β​x)m)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int{\frac{x^{n}}{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{-q}}dx}=\int{\sum\limits_{m=1}^{-q}\left(\frac{A_{m}}{(1+\alpha x)^{m}}+\frac{B_{m}}{(1+\beta x)^{m}}\right)dx} (4.9)
    =A1​ln⁡(1+α​x)α+B1​ln⁡(1+β​x)β+∑m=2−q(Amα⁡(1−m)​(1+α​x)m−1+Bmβ⁡(1−m)​(1+β​x)m−1).\displaystyle=A_{1}\frac{\ln(1+\alpha x)}{\alpha}+B_{1}\frac{\ln(1+\beta x)}{\beta}+\sum\limits_{m=2}^{-q}\left(\frac{A_{m}}{\alpha(1-m)(1+\alpha x)^{m-1}}+\frac{B_{m}}{\beta(1-m)(1+\beta x)^{m-1}}\right).

    In other words, the result consists of a sum of rational functions and logarithmic terms. The only scenario in which (4.9) can be algebraic is if A1=B1=0A_{1}=B_{1}=0. The coefficients A1A_{1} and B1B_{1} can be computed either via the generalized residue formula:

    A1=1(−q−1)!​d−q−1d​x−q−1​[xn(1+β​x)−q]|x=−1α≠0,A_{1}=\frac{1}{(-q-1)!}\left.\frac{d^{\,-q-1}}{dx^{\,-q-1}}\Bigl[\frac{x^{n}}{(1+\beta x)^{-q}}\Bigr]\right|_{x=-\frac{1}{\alpha}}\neq 0,
    B1=1(−q−1)!​d−q−1d​x−q−1​[xn(1+α​x)−q]|x=−1β≠0.B_{1}=\frac{1}{(-q-1)!}\left.\frac{d^{\,-q-1}}{dx^{\,-q-1}}\Bigl[\frac{x^{n}}{(1+\alpha x)^{-q}}\Bigr]\right|_{x=-\frac{1}{\beta}}\neq 0.

    or symbolically, as they naturally arise when integrating rational functions, for instance using Hermite reduction [gG13, Chapter 22]. This is a standard and largely automated procedure in computer algebra systems.

Remark 4.9.

Although the case b0=0b_{0}=0 falls outside the class we are considering, it is still easy to treat. S⁡(x)S(x) writes as

S⁡(x)=(a2​x2+a1​x+1)−1−b1a1​(((a1+b1)​s0+s1)​∫(a2​x2+a1​x+1)b1a1+c1).S(x)=(a_{2}x^{2}+a_{1}x+1)^{-1-\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}}\left(((a_{1}+b_{1})s_{0}+s_{1})\int(a_{2}x^{2}+a_{1}x+1)^{\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}}+c_{1}\right).

Hence, if b1a1∈ℕ\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}\in\mathbb{N} or b1a1+32∈−ℕ\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}+\frac{3}{2}\in-\mathbb{N}, then C1 by the analysis performed for n=0n=0. Otherwise, C3 with (1,−a1−b1)(1,-a_{1}-b_{1}).

4.2.2 Transcendence in both components.

‘‘Though this be madness, yet there is method in’t.’’
— W. Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act II, Scene II.

Even if both I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} are transcendental, the linear combination

b0​s0​I1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​I2b_{0}s_{0}I_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})I_{2}

might still be algebraic. In this section, we provide an algorithm to detect such cases.

  1. 1.

    𝐪∉−ℕ∗,𝐪+𝟑𝟐∉−ℕ\mathbf{q\notin-\mathbb{N}^{*},q+\frac{3}{2}\notin-\mathbb{N}}. Then, by Lemma 4.6:

    I1\displaystyle I_{1} =cI​∫(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​𝑑x+C1​(x)​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q+1,\displaystyle=c_{I}\int{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}+C_{1}(x)(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q+1},
    I2\displaystyle I_{2} =cI​I​∫(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​𝑑x+C2​(x)​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q+1.\displaystyle=c_{II}\int{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}+C_{2}(x)(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q+1}.

    The transcendence of I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} means two things: ∫(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​𝑑x\int{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx} is transcendental, and cI,cI​I≠0c_{I},c_{II}\neq 0. So

    b0​s0​I1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​I2=\displaystyle b_{0}s_{0}I_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})I_{2}=
    =(b0​s0​cI+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​cI​I)​∫(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​dx⏟transcendental+\displaystyle=(b_{0}s_{0}c_{I}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})c_{II})\underbrace{\int{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}}_{\text{transcendental}}+
    +(b0​s0​C1​(x)+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​C2​(x))​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q+1⏟algebraic.\displaystyle+\underbrace{(b_{0}s_{0}C_{1}(x)+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})C_{2}(x))(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q+1}}_{\text{algebraic}}.

    can only be algebraic if

    b0​s0​cI+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​cI​I=0,b_{0}s_{0}c_{I}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})c_{II}=0,

    which rewrites as

    s1=s0​(b0​cI+a1​cI​I+b1​cI​I)(b0+1)​cI​I.s_{1}=\frac{s_{0}(b_{0}c_{I}+a_{1}c_{II}+b_{1}c_{II})}{(b_{0}+1)c_{II}}.

    Hence, we are in C3 and the algorithm returns (cI​I​(b0+1),b0​cI+a1​cI​I+b1​cI​I)(c_{II}(b_{0}+1),b_{0}c_{I}+a_{1}c_{II}+b_{1}c_{II}).

  2. 2.

    𝐪+𝟑𝟐∈−ℕ\mathbf{q+\frac{3}{2}\in-\mathbb{N}}.

    Each of I1I_{1}, I2I_{2} can be written in the form

    c​∫(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​dx⏟algebraic+c~​∫x−2​q−1​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​dx⏟transcendental+C⁡(x)​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q+1⏟algebraic,c\underbrace{\int{(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}}_{\text{algebraic}}+\tilde{c}\underbrace{\int{x^{-2q-1}(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}}_{\text{transcendental}}+\underbrace{C(x)(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q+1}}_{\text{algebraic}},

    where the constant c~\tilde{c} will be denoted as c~1\tilde{c}_{1} (respectively, c~2\tilde{c}_{2}) for I1I_{1}(respectively, I2I_{2}). Hence,

    b0​s0​I1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​I2\displaystyle b_{0}s_{0}I_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})I_{2}
    =(b0​s0​c~1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​c~2)​∫x−2​q−1​(1+a1​x+a2​x2)q​𝑑x+𝒜⁡(x).\displaystyle=(b_{0}s_{0}\tilde{c}_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})\tilde{c}_{2})\int{x^{-2q-1}(1+a_{1}x+a_{2}x^{2})^{q}dx}+\mathcal{A}(x).

    where 𝒜⁡(x)\mathcal{A}(x) is some algebraic function. Similarly to the previous case, we are in C3 and the algorithm returns (c~2​(b0+1),b0​c~1+a1​c~2+b1​c~2)(\tilde{c}_{2}(b_{0}+1),b_{0}\tilde{c}_{1}+a_{1}\tilde{c}_{2}+b_{1}\tilde{c}_{2}).

  3. 3.

    𝐪∈−ℕ∗\mathbf{q\in-\mathbb{N}^{*}}. Then

    I1=A1(1)​ln⁡(1+α​x)α+B1(1)​ln⁡(1+β​x)β+𝒜1​(x),\displaystyle I_{1}=A_{1}^{(1)}\frac{\ln(1+\alpha x)}{\alpha}+B_{1}^{(1)}\frac{\ln(1+\beta x)}{\beta}+\mathcal{A}_{1}(x),
    I2=A1(2)​ln⁡(1+α​x)α+B1(2)​ln⁡(1+β​x)β+𝒜2​(x).\displaystyle I_{2}=A_{1}^{(2)}\frac{\ln(1+\alpha x)}{\alpha}+B_{1}^{(2)}\frac{\ln(1+\beta x)}{\beta}+\mathcal{A}_{2}(x).

    where 𝒜1​(x),𝒜2​(x)\mathcal{A}_{1}(x),\mathcal{A}_{2}(x) are some algebraic functions. So

    b0​s0​I1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​I2\displaystyle b_{0}s_{0}I_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})I_{2} =(b0​s0​A1(1)+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​A1(2))​ln⁡(1+α​x)α\displaystyle=(b_{0}s_{0}A_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})A_{1}^{(2)})\frac{\ln(1+\alpha x)}{\alpha}
    +(b0​s0​B1(1)+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​B1(2))​ln⁡(1+β​x)β\displaystyle+(b_{0}s_{0}B_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})B_{1}^{(2)})\frac{\ln(1+\beta x)}{\beta}
    +𝒜⁡(x).\displaystyle+\mathcal{A}(x).

    Equivalently,

    b0​s0​I1+(a1​s0+b0​s1+b1​s0+s1)​I2\displaystyle b_{0}s_{0}I_{1}+(a_{1}s_{0}+b_{0}s_{1}+b_{1}s_{0}+s_{1})I_{2} =(s0​(b0​A1(1)+a1​A1(2)+b1​A1(2))+s1​A1(2)​(b0+1))​ln⁡(1+α​x)α\displaystyle=(s_{0}(b_{0}A_{1}^{(1)}+a_{1}A_{1}^{(2)}+b_{1}A_{1}^{(2)})+s_{1}A_{1}^{(2)}(b_{0}+1))\frac{\ln(1+\alpha x)}{\alpha}
    +(s0​(b0​B1(1)+a1​B1(2)+b1​B1(2))+s1​B1(2)​(b0+1))​ln⁡(1+β​x)β\displaystyle+(s_{0}(b_{0}B_{1}^{(1)}+a_{1}B_{1}^{(2)}+b_{1}B_{1}^{(2)})+s_{1}B_{1}^{(2)}(b_{0}+1))\frac{\ln(1+\beta x)}{\beta}
    +𝒜⁡(x).\displaystyle+\mathcal{A}(x).

    which is algebraic if and only if the coefficients multiplying the logarithmic terms are simultaneously equal to zero (we recall that α≠β\alpha\neq\beta). In other words, one needs

    (b0​A1(1)+(a1+b1)​A1(2)(b0+1)​A1(2)b0​B1(1)+(a1+b1)​B1(2)(b0+1)​B1(2))​(s0s1)=(00).\begin{pmatrix}b_{0}A_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})A_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)A_{1}^{(2)}\\ b_{0}B_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})B_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)B_{1}^{(2)}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}s_{0}\\ s_{1}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ 0\end{pmatrix}.

    Hence, we are in C3 if the matrix

    ℳ=(b0​A1(1)+(a1+b1)​A1(2)(b0+1)​A1(2)b0​B1(1)+(a1+b1)​B1(2)(b0+1)​B1(2))\mathcal{M}=\begin{pmatrix}b_{0}A_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})A_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)A_{1}^{(2)}\\ b_{0}B_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})B_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)B_{1}^{(2)}\end{pmatrix}

    is not invertible. Then the algorithm returns a nonzero element of its kernel. Otherwise, the conclusion is C2.

4.2.3 Examples

  1. 1.

    Motzkin numbers (OEIS A001006).

    The recurrence

    (n+2)​mn=(2​n+1)​mn−1+(3​n−3)​mn−2(n+2)m_{n}=(2n+1)m_{n-1}+(3n-3)m_{n-2}

    corresponds to

    b0=2,a1=−2,b1=−1,a2=−3,b2=3.b_{0}=2,a_{1}=-2,b_{1}=-1,a_{2}=-3,b_{2}=3.

    We have b2=2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}=\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}}, a12−4​a2≠0a_{1}^{2}-4a_{2}\neq 0, b0∈ℕ∗b_{0}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Moreover, q=−b0+b1a1=−32⟹q+32=0∈−ℕq=-b_{0}+\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}=-\frac{3}{2}\implies q+\frac{3}{2}=0\in-\mathbb{N}.

    I1=∫x​(1−2​x−3​x2)−32​𝑑x,I2=∫x2​(1−2​x−3​x2)−32​𝑑x.I_{1}=\int{x(1-2x-3x^{2})^{-\frac{3}{2}}dx},\qquad I_{2}=\int{x^{2}(1-2x-3x^{2})^{-\frac{3}{2}}dx}.

    b0−1=1<−2​q−1=2⟹b_{0}-1=1<-2q-1=2\implies I1I_{1} is algebraic.
    b0=2=−2​q−1⟹b_{0}=2=-2q-1\implies I2I_{2} is transcendental.

    The algorithm returns C3 with (b0+1,−(a1+b1))=(3,3)(b_{0}+1,-(a_{1}+b_{1}))=(3,3), proving that Motzkin-type sequences are globally bounded if and only if the two first terms coincide.

    Alternatively, one can verify the transcendence of any solution with m0≠m1m_{0}\neq m_{1} by initializing the recurrence with, for instance, m0=0,m1=1m_{0}=0,m_{1}=1, converting it into a homogeneous differential equation, and then using the istranscendental function from Maple’s gfun package (available since version 4.10).

  2. 2.

    Central trinomial coefficients (OEIS A002426).

    The recurrence

    n​sn=(2​n−1)​sn−1+(3​n−3)​sn−2ns_{n}=(2n-1)s_{n-1}+(3n-3)s_{n-2}

    corresponds to

    b0=0,a1=−2,b1=1,a2=−3,b2=3.b_{0}=0,a_{1}=-2,b_{1}=1,a_{2}=-3,b_{2}=3.

    We have b2=2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}=\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}}, a12−4​a2≠0a_{1}^{2}-4a_{2}\neq 0. b0=0b_{0}=0, so we look at b1a1=−12\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}=-\frac{1}{2}. Since b1a1=12∉ℕ\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}=\frac{1}{2}\notin\mathbb{N} and b1a1+32=1∉−ℕ\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}+\frac{3}{2}=1\notin-\mathbb{N}, the algorithm returns C3 with (1,−(a1+b1))=(1,1)(1,-(a_{1}+b_{1}))=(1,1).

    This is consistent with the fact that s0=s1=1s_{0}=s_{1}=1 yields not just an almost integral, but an integer sequence of the Central trinomial coefficients. In particular, we deduce that the only integer sequences satisfying the recurrence for the central trinomial coefficients are those with s0=s1s_{0}=s_{1}, mirroring the case of Motzkin numbers.

  3. 3.

    Large Schröder numbers (OEIS A006318) : fully algebraic example.

    The recurrence

    (n+1)​sn=(6​n−3)​sn−1−(n−2)​sn−2(n+1)s_{n}=(6n-3)s_{n-1}-(n-2)s_{n-2}

    corresponds to

    b0=1,a1=−6,b1=3,a2=1,b2=−2.b_{0}=1,a_{1}=-6,b_{1}=3,a_{2}=1,b_{2}=-2.

    We have b2=2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}=\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}}, a12−4​a2≠0a_{1}^{2}-4a_{2}\neq 0, b0∈ℕ∗b_{0}\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Moreover, q=−b0+b1a1=−32⟹q+32∈ℕq=-b_{0}+\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}=-\frac{3}{2}\implies q+\frac{3}{2}\in\mathbb{N}.

    I1=∫(1−6​x+x2)−32​𝑑x,I2=∫x​(1−6​x+x2)−32​𝑑x.I_{1}=\int{(1-6x+x^{2})^{-\frac{3}{2}}dx},\qquad I_{2}=\int{x(1-6x+x^{2})^{-\frac{3}{2}}dx}.

    b0−1=0<−2​q−1=2⟹b_{0}-1=0<-2q-1=2\implies I1I_{1} is algebraic.
    b0=1=−2​q−1⟹b_{0}=1=-2q-1\implies I2I_{2} is algebraic.

    The algorithm returns C1.

  4. 4.

    Fully transcendental example.

    Consider the following innocent-looking recurrence:

    (n+3)​sn=(n+1)​sn−1+(2​n−2)​sn−2.(n+3)s_{n}=(n+1)s_{n-1}+(2n-2)s_{n-2}.

    It corresponds to

    b0=3,a1=−1,b1=−1,a2=−2,b2=2.b_{0}=3,a_{1}=-1,b_{1}=-1,a_{2}=-2,b_{2}=2.

    We have b2=2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}=\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}}, a12−4​a2≠0a_{1}^{2}-4a_{2}\neq 0, b0∈ℕ∗b_{0}\in\mathbb{N}^{*} and q=−b0+b1a1=−2∈−ℕ∗q=-b_{0}+\frac{b_{1}}{a_{1}}=-2\in-\mathbb{N}^{*}.

    I1=∫x2(1−x−2​x2)2​𝑑x=227​ln⁡(2​x−1)−227​ln⁡(x+1)−118​(2​x−1)−19​(x+1),I_{1}=\int{\frac{x^{2}}{(1-x-2x^{2})^{2}}dx}=\frac{2}{27}\ln(2x-1)-\frac{2}{27}\ln(x+1)-\frac{1}{18(2x-1)}-\frac{1}{9(x+1)},
    I2=∫x3(1−x−2​x2)2​𝑑x=7108​ln⁡(2​x−1)+527​ln⁡(x+1)−136​(2​x−1)+19​(x+1).I_{2}=\int{\frac{x^{3}}{(1-x-2x^{2})^{2}}dx}=\frac{7}{108}\ln(2x-1)+\frac{5}{27}\ln(x+1)-\frac{1}{36(2x-1)}+\frac{1}{9(x+1)}.

    So,

    A1(1)=227,B1(1)=−227,A1(2)=7108,B1(2)=527.A_{1}^{(1)}=\frac{2}{27},\ B_{1}^{(1)}=-\frac{2}{27},\ A_{1}^{(2)}=\frac{7}{108},\ B_{1}^{(2)}=\frac{5}{27}.

    None of these numbers are equal to zero, in particular this implies that both I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} are transcendental. Moreover, the matrix

    (b0​A1(1)+(a1+b1)​A1(2)(b0+1)​A1(2)b0​B1(1)+(a1+b1)​B1(2)(b0+1)​B1(2))=(5/547/27−16/2720/27).\begin{pmatrix}b_{0}A_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})A_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)A_{1}^{(2)}\\ b_{0}B_{1}^{(1)}+(a_{1}+b_{1})B_{1}^{(2)}&(b_{0}+1)B_{1}^{(2)}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5/54&7/27\\ -16/27&20/27\end{pmatrix}.

    is invertible, as its determinant equals 29≠0\frac{2}{9}\neq 0. Hence, no choice of s0,s1s_{0},s_{1} can make S⁡(x)=∑n≥0sn​xnS(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}s_{n}x^{n} algebraic. The algorithm returns C2.

5 Integrality revisited

‘‘Coming back to where you started is not the same as never leaving.’’
— T. Pratchett, A Hat Full of Sky.

Although proving algebraicity does not directly address the problem of finding integer solutions to a recurrence, it often greatly simplifies the analysis. In the specific setting of second-order recurrences of the form

(n+b0)​sn+(a1​n+b1)​sn−1+(a2​n+b2)​sn−2=0(n+b_{0})s_{n}+(a_{1}n+b_{1})s_{n-1}+(a_{2}n+b_{2})s_{n-2}=0

with b2=2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}=\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}}, integrality implies global boundedness, which in turn is equivalent to algebraicity. Thus, the problem of deciding whether a solution is integral reduces to detecting algebraicity — something that can be done using the algorithm developed in Section 4 (see Fig. 3). Analysing integrality within this algebraic framework is generally easier.

For instance, if an algebraic solution has a closed-form expression involving rational powers of polynomials, its integrality can be established using the criteria derived by Pomerat and Straub in [PS24] (Theorem 1.1 and multiple examples applied to specific cases).

Example.

Consider a recurrence relation:

n​sn+(2​n+3)​sn−1+9​(n+3)​sn−2=0.ns_{n}+(2n+3)s_{n-1}+9(n+3)s_{n-2}=0. (5)

Applying our algorithm (note that b0=0b_{0}=0), we find that S⁡(x)=∑n≥0sn​xnS(x)=\sum\limits_{n\geq 0}s_{n}x^{n} is globally bounded if and only if s1=−5​s0s_{1}=-5s_{0}. In that case, one has

S⁡(x)=s0​(1+2​x+9​x2)−52.S(x)=s_{0}(1+2x+9x^{2})^{-\frac{5}{2}}.

Clearly, all integral solutions are among the globally bounded ones. Thus, the problem reduces to identifying the values of s0s_{0} for which s0​(1+2​x+9​x2)−52s_{0}(1+2x+9x^{2})^{-\frac{5}{2}} lies in ℤ⁡[[x]]\mathbb{Z}[[x]].

Proposition 5.1.

If s0∈ℤs_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}, then

s0​(1+2​x+9​x2)−52∈ℤ⁡[[x]].s_{0}(1+2x+9x^{2})^{-\frac{5}{2}}\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]].
Proof.

The claim is a direct consequence of the following result:

Lemma 5.2.

([PS24, Example 1.8]) Let a,b∈ℤ,λ∈ℚa,b\in\mathbb{Z},\ \lambda\in\mathbb{Q}. Let kk be the denominator of λ\lambda brought to the lowest terms. Then (1+a​x+b​x2)λ∈ℤ⁡[[x]](1+ax+bx^{2})^{\lambda}\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]] if and only if

  • •

    a,b∈k​r​a​d​(k)​ℤa,b\in k\ rad(k)\mathbb{Z}, or

  • •

    k=2​κk=2\kappa and a,b∈κ​r​a​d​(κ)​ℤa,b\in\kappa\ rad(\kappa)\mathbb{Z} as well as (a,b)≡(2,1)(a,b)\equiv(2,1) (mod 4).

Here r​a​d​(k)rad(k) denotes the largest squarefree integer dividing kk (for example, r​a​d​(24)=6rad(24)=6).

In our setting a=2,b=9,λ=−52,k=2,κ=1a=2,b=9,\lambda=-\frac{5}{2},k=2,\kappa=1. Since 2,9∈ℤ2,9\in\mathbb{Z} and (2,9)≡(2,1)(2,9)\equiv(2,1) (mod 4) we get (1+2​x+9​x2)−52∈ℤ⁡[[x]](1+2x+9x^{2})^{-\frac{5}{2}}\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]]. Hence, for any s0∈ℤs_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}, s0​(1+2​x+9​x2)−52∈ℤ⁡[[x]]s_{0}(1+2x+9x^{2})^{-\frac{5}{2}}\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]]. ∎

Since taking s0∉ℤs_{0}\notin\mathbb{Z} would already violate the condition sn∈ℤ​ for all ​n∈ℕs_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}\ \text{ for all }n\in\mathbb{N}, we conclude that S⁡(x)∈ℤ⁡[[x]]S(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[[x]] if and only if s1=−5​s0s_{1}=-5s_{0} and s0∈ℤs_{0}\in\mathbb{Z}.

6 Integrality criteria for small Apéry numbers

In this section, we investigate the sequences (an)n(a_{n})_{n} satisfying the recurrence relation

n2​an=(11​n2−11​n+3)​an−1+(n−1)2​an−2,n≥2.n^{2}a_{n}=(11n^{2}-11n+3)a_{n-1}+(n-1)^{2}a_{n-2},\quad n\geq 2. (5.1)

In the standard setting, this recurrence is initialized with a0=1,a1=3a_{0}=1,a_{1}=3, yielding the sequence of small Apéry numbers (OEIS A005258). These numbers also admit a binomial sum representation:

an=∑k=0n(nk)2​(n+kk),a_{n}=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{n+k}{k}, (5.2)

which makes it clear that they are all integers. However, the situation becomes more complex when considering arbitrary initial conditions. Let (a​(μ,λ)n)n(a(\mu,\lambda)_{n})_{n} denote the solution of (5.1) with a0=μ,a1=λa_{0}=\mu,a_{1}=\lambda. The behaviour of these generalized Apéry-type sequences is described in the following theorem, which, to the best of our knowledge, is new, though similar to the case of big Apéry numbers (OEIS A005259).

Theorem 6.1.

A sequence of rational numbers (an)n(a_{n})_{n} satisfying (5.1) is integral if and only if (a0,a1)=(α,3​α)(a_{0},a_{1})=(\alpha,3\alpha) for α∈ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

Let us first show that a​(1,3)n∈ℤa(1,3)_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n≥0n\geq 0. Obviously, this would imply that a​(α,3​α)n∈ℤa(\alpha,3\alpha)_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n≥0,α∈ℤn\geq 0,\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}.
The sequence (a~n)n(\tilde{a}_{n})_{n} defined by a~n=∑k=0n(nk)2​(n+kk)\tilde{a}_{n}=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{n+k}{k} is a solution to (5.1) (a result due to Apéry). While coming up with such a relation is nontrivial, its verification is straightforward with creative telescoping techniques [Zei91]. In Maple this can be done by calling Zeilberger function from the SumTools/Hypergeometric package, which applies Zeilberger’s algorithm to find a recurrence satisfied by a given binomial sum.

> A := binomial(n, k)^2 * binomial(n + k, k):
> simplify(SumTools[Hypergeometric][Zeilberger](A, n, k, a_n)[1]);
(n+2)2​an2+(−11​n2−33​n−25)​an−(n+1)2,(n+2)^{2}a_{n}^{2}+(-11n^{2}-33n-25)a_{n}-(n+1)^{2},

where the powers of ana_{n} correspond to the coefficient shift, i.e. the expression above is equivalent to

(n+2)2​an+2−(11​(n+2)2−11​(n+2)+3)​an+1−(n+1)2​an=0,n≥0(n+2)^{2}a_{n+2}-(11(n+2)^{2}-11(n+2)+3)a_{n+1}-(n+1)^{2}a_{n}=0,\quad n\geq 0

which is simply a shift of (5.1).

In addition, every a~n\tilde{a}_{n} is a sum of binomials, hence an integer. We check the first two values:

a~0=(00)2​(00)=1,\displaystyle\tilde{a}_{0}=\binom{0}{0}^{2}\binom{0}{0}=1,
a~1=(10)2​(10)+(11)2​(21)=1+2=3.\displaystyle\tilde{a}_{1}=\binom{1}{0}^{2}\binom{1}{0}+\binom{1}{1}^{2}\binom{2}{1}=1+2=3.

Since any solution of (5.1) is uniquely defined by a pair of initial values (a0,a1a_{0},a_{1}), we deduce that (a​(1,3)n)n=(a~n)n(a(1,3)_{n})_{n}=(\tilde{a}_{n})_{n}. Thus, (a​(1,3)n)n(a(1,3)_{n})_{n} is indeed integral. ∎

We now present two proofs that establish the uniqueness of this integral solution.

6.1 Proof 1

For every n≥2n\geq 2

an=(11​n2−11​n+3)n2​an−1+(n−1)2n2​an−2.a_{n}=\frac{(11n^{2}-11n+3)}{n^{2}}a_{n-1}+\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}}a_{n-2}. (5.3)

Consider two sequences (un)n(u_{n})_{n} and (vn)n(v_{n})_{n} defined by

un=(11​n2−11​n+3)n2,vn=(n−1)2n2u_{n}=\frac{(11n^{2}-11n+3)}{n^{2}},\quad v_{n}=\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}}

for all n≥0n\geq 0. Then (5.3) becomes

an=un​an−1+vn​an−2.a_{n}=u_{n}a_{n-1}+v_{n}a_{n-2}. (5.4)

The following result by Chang [Cha84] proves to be remarkably useful in our setting.

Theorem 6.2.

([Cha84]): Suppose that

Theorem 6.2 is naturally applicable to certain 2-order P-recursive sequences. In particular, it can be used to prove the uniqueness of an integer solution should one exist. The following reasoning mimics the one for big Apéry numbers in [Cha84], presented as an application of Theorem 6.1 in [Cha84].

Let us prove the ⟹\implies direction of Theorem 6.1 by contradiction. Assume there exist μ,λ∈ℤ\mu,\lambda\in\mathbb{Z} with λ≠3​μ\lambda\neq 3\mu such that a​(μ,λ)n∈ℤa(\mu,\lambda)_{n}\in\mathbb{Z} for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Then all the conditions of Theorem 6.2 are satisfied. Indeed, for all k>2k>2

vk=(k−1)2k2≠0v_{k}=\frac{(k-1)^{2}}{k^{2}}\neq 0

limn→∞∏k=2n|vk|=limn→∞∏k=2n(k−1)2k2=limn→∞1n2=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\prod_{k=2}^{n}|v_{k}|=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\prod_{k=2}^{n}\frac{(k-1)^{2}}{k^{2}}=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{n^{2}}=0.

Therefore, (5.1) has at most 1 integral solution, and we have already seen that it is given by (a​(1,3)n)n(a(1,3)_{n})_{n}.

This proof is largely inspired by the work of André-Jeannin [AJ91] on the integrality of big Apéry numbers.

7 Concluding remarks

The story, however, is far from complete, as several questions remain open. The case of b2≠2​a2​b1−a1​a2​b0a1b_{2}\neq\frac{2a_{2}b_{1}-a_{1}a_{2}b_{0}}{a_{1}} is still poorly understood, although we believe it leads to not globally bounded solutions. Moreover, our algorithm is currently not applicable to the recurrences with b0∉ℕb_{0}\notin\mathbb{N}. Beyond that, higher-order recurrences or those with nonlinear polynomial coefficients present further challenges. Their solution spaces are more complex, and the connection between global boundedness and algebraicity becomes harder to characterise.

Although our main goal was to decide algebraicity and global boundedness, the original question of integrality motivated much of this work. By revealing a structural connection between these notions for second-order recurrences, we were able to approach parts of the integrality problem via concepts from differential algebra. This perspective not only simplifies the analysis, but also suggests a path toward a more systematic, algorithmic treatment of arithmetic properties in holonomic sequences.
